title: A Great Game, But Only If You're Hardcore
text:
What made the Metal Gear series so wonderful was the concept of a lone operative sneaking into a base a la James Bond, but doing it realistically (crawling, hiding, sniping) instead of getting invited to a white-tie dinner by the bad guy. In the first PS1 game, you could be a novice player and still make it through the game, each time you play making you better and better. The PS2 games got more and more complex, sort of bloating up the concept with more complex controls and quick reaction scenarios where the average player would get creamed over and over again until the learning curve was passed. These "frustration points," as I call them got more and more numerous until MGS3, where the entire last third of the game was essentially one long frustration point (e.g., oops, stepped wrong, you die, oops, didn't make the shot, you die, oops, didn't lead the girl through 5 screens of bad guys safely, start over, etc.) To a hardcore gamer, these challenges are meat and potatoes, but to a casual gamer that can't play daily, the fourteenth time that 3 Metal Gears blow Snake into atoms is the time that the game gets shelved permanently. This is where MGS:Portable Ops puts itself: it's JUST hard enough to make the hardcore MGS fans want more, but JUST hard enough to frustrate the casual gamer into just shelving it.

First off, the game looks great and the sounds are perfect. How they crammed all of this into a UMD is spectacular and shows how well software developers can compensate for poorly-designed hardware. The controls aren't too bad, but the analog nub can be hard to control at times. The real permanent frustration point in the game comes with the camera, which seems to have a mind of its own. Dragging enemies (a HUGE part of the game) becomes a comedy of errors as the whirling camera causes you to spin around while you get used to the analog nub...you look like you're tangoing with a drunken partner! The camera likes to sit right up against your active man, so you can't pan out and get a wider view of things...this is especially fatal when going through doors, where you can see an all clear and pop out right into a guard's line of fire. For me, the camera is enough to make the game unpleasant...but I suppose it can be gotten used to. The missions are broken up into little ones (UMD format again) and they seem fine. They make sense and you do have some sense of time in the game. Well done!

MGS games are all about sneaking and infiltrating. Well, this MGS takes it one step further by allowing you to recruit soldiers for different teams (this has been explained in other reviews.) This is sort of a tactics-style development where you can outfit the troops, put them in squads and deploy them as a team. However, the developers decided to hamstring this potentially fun feature by making it so killed soldiers never return...so you can get a secret character for a major accomplishment...and he gets an unlucky camera angle on the next mission and ends up getting jumped by 3 guards. Well, your hard-earned man is now gone forever unless you reload. By making the risk too great, this keeps casual gamers from risking hard-earned troops on the battlefield. They should have an option for an easier mode where the soldiers can be brought back. However, the saving grace is that the unique characters (such as Snake) can be brought back and recover slowly.

This game is very complex and mastering it, or even proceeding in it takes a large time investment...unfortunately, it's not one that most casual or older gamers might be able to make. The manual only tells you how things work on a basic level and, like ALL NEW GAMES TODAY, you can't just have fun and play through...you've got to have the FAQ/game guide/cheat sheet with you or you'll never get 100% complete and the best ending. Lame.

With very little to reward the casual gamer, I can't recommend this as a 5-star pick. I'd rate it a 1. However, since it's so appealing by its tough nature to hardcore gamers (5 stars for them!), it DOES merit a 3 on the fun factor (1+5/2). The polish of the game is super and only the whirly camera demon knocks it down to 4 stars.

title: Pretty, But Flawed
text:
This game is lush, rich with color and has graphics that will go down forever as some of the best that Square-Enix has ever produced. The game mechanics are sound and more like the online FFXI (no loading screens for every battle!) but the game, like most Final Fantasies, loses its lustre about halfway through.

The numerous other reviews cover the pros and cons of the game in detail so I won't repeat them here. What I WILL say, though, is that the designers seem to always want the gamers to lose interest in their game 50% of the way through. For example, if you've enjoyed the game up to the 5 mandragora fight, the frustration and irritation will be enough to make you quit. It's one thing if there's a strategy or some tactic to use and discover, but this fight is just a borefest of repetitively hitting one monster, watching your entire party get hit with 5 status effects simultaneously and having them lose 80% of their HP. You barely survive, inflict a scratch or two on one of the 5 monsters...and repeat, repeat, repeat. After 3 hours of this, I had enough. title: Ignore the Subject Matter...This Game Is Just Plain Fun!
text:
OK, just ignore the fact that this game is Pokemon-based for a moment. DS games are fun because the stylus allows for new types of gameplay and games that use this feature in novel ways are fast becoming a trademark for Nintendo, who can sell truckloads of DS units for each PSP that is sold. Why? Well, rather than try to make PS2 games work on a tiny unit that can't process the polygons or duplicate the controls, Nintendo wisely decided to make new, fun games for the DS and leave direct ports to GBA carts that DS owners could also pick up if they want some old-school action. This concept of fun leads into the review of Pokemon Rangers.

The premise is fairly easy, since Pokemon products are targeted at kids. You're a male or female Pokemon Ranger neophyte, fresh in from the sticks and ready for training. Your job is to basically assist people and Pokemon whenever they need it and defend Pokemon from greedy and neglectful individuals. The intro is a bit long, but it's good to get the basics and story down. You have a special Ranger tool called the "Capture Styler" that can, with your effort and goodwill, impart a calming emotion to wild or upset Pokemon and calm them down. This is the entire capturing concept. Once you've captured the Pokemon, its info is registered in the browser on the top screen and you can have the Pokemon follow you around. Captured Pokemon can be used in several ways: certain Pokemon have "field moves" that can break rocks, cut fences, grapple posts to pull you across water and so on. Most Pokemon can also assist you in capturing by enhancing your styler with powers (e.g., grass assist makes your styler trail into grass, which stops Pokemon that touch it) and the electric Pokemon can recharge your styler. This recharge capability becomes critical later on, as there is no real violence, but Pokemon can attack your styler line and damage it (0 styler energy=game over) and having a refill is always handy. The kicker to this entire concept of using Pokemon is that, in the interest of not exploiting the Pokemon unfairly, you can only use their power once. The only exception is your personal Pokemon, which you can charge up and use over and over. Additionally, you may only have a limited number of captured Pokemon at one time and you have to let them free whenever you leave their native area. This makes for some serious strategy, as you have to balance their usefulness in capturing with the necessity to clear obstacles with their field moves. Also, do you carry a bunch of recharge Pokemon and only one field move one or do you balance out your herd with a battle-useful one, a recharge one and maybe a couple of field-useful ones? This element is a welcome change of pace from the usual "your gun can always fire unlimited bullets, just go get this one key and run across the map to unlock the door." In this game, if you choose wisely, you can have a herd assembled and just blaze through obstacles.

This game offers no real violence, as said before. The "battles" are just capture sessions with no real time limit. The Pokemon (one or more) appear in the bottom screen and immediately begin to amble, fly or ooze about. Most of them have attacks that randomly go off and some can respond to seeing the styler capture loop...the trick is to time the capture correctly and avoid damage to the styler. It gets progressively harder, forcing you to not just draw stupid circles all day, but wait and figure out patterns, try new strategies and take risks. I'm sure it can get old after 4 or 5 hours straight, but in short doses, this is a welcome change of pace.

The only real downside to the game is the sound. The music is lame and the Pokemon make generic-sounding shrieks or cries instead of saying their name like they do in the cartoons. The graphics are cartoonish, but fairly sharp and you can interact with a lot of objects. The bottom screen holds all of the interaction and the top is taken up by the Stylus radar screen, so it's good use of the DS real estate.

This game is good for kids because it teaches them resource management, hand-eye coordination and risk taking and does so in a very kid-friendly manner that doesn't involve blood, gore and foul language. For adults, the premise and graphics might seem puerile, but the game IS fun in doses and is great for a breaktime distraction.

This game is worth getting, in my opinion. There's just too much fun and strategy to be had in such a small package.

title: Updated, But Never Overrated or Outdated
text:
I remember buying FF2/4 the day it came out and playing it for 12 straight hours. The combination of the graphics and lush (for that time) scenery was almost too much to handle and the music is STILL stuck in my head to this day. Much like FF3/6, this game is one of the classics that's in the Top 10 RPGs of ALL time. Here is a breakdown of the game according to my rating system, with the original being the perfect standard:

Graphics: The GBA/DS doesn't disappoint with the sharper resolution and what seems to be slightly enhanced colors. The portrait redraws are OK and the sprites all seemed to have at least been retouched with some more saturation. The Mode 7 effects and all the magic effects are still the same. There wasn't much improvement in this area and since GBA games are almost direct copies of SNES games, this isn't a big deal. I was a little disappointed that they didn't add some richer textures and patterns in the games to make it sort of like the eye-popping visuals of FF3/6, but since it copies the original, that's OK. 8 out of 10

Sound: This is where the limitation of the GBA hardware comes into play. The sounds are tinny, with none of that rumbly bass the SNES sound engine had (even with high quality headphones.) The songs haven't been changed, but they're running through a different wavetable and it is obvious to those who remember the old SNES sounds. It's still good, though. This is one of the nicest soundtracks ever made to a game and it holds up well to anything today. 7 out of 10

Translation: I've played the full Japanese and original versions and I have to say that I am both pleasantly and unpleasantly surprised by the new dialogue. While it DOES flow smoothly and articles are in place (i.e., THE Sand Ruby, instead of Sand Ruby), the translation takes minor liberties with the dialogue that can sort of spoil the original feel. For example, fans of the original will be disappointed to learn that the magic spells are changed from FIRE 1, FIRE 2, FIRE 3 to the modern standard of Fire, Fira and Firaga. It's not a huge deal, but I kind of miss the old names. While "spoony bard" is still there, the package from the original is replaced with Bomb Ring. Part of the mystery and sadness of Mysidia's destruction was that Cecil and Kain had no idea what was in the package and were just dupes. Well...if you can't guess what a BOMB RING does, then you are as dull as a...well, Dark Knight's buttplate. The text can be tiny at times...for old folks like me with bad eyesight, this can be troublesome. Overall, the story hasn't changed and is as good as ever. 7 out of 10

Gameplay: This is where the game shines, as nothing has been subtracted from the original. Rather, things have been added: easier gameplay through the first half, additonal dungeons, and bestiary. 10 out of 10.

If you liked the SNES version and need a portable one, then you need this game. However, unlike FFI&II: Dawn of Souls, you're not getting a huge upgrade over the original and, in cases like the music, you're getting a little shortchanged. If you don't need this to take on a trip, I'd recommend just playing the SNES version. I know I still have mine!

Overall, I'd highly recommend this: 32 out of 40. Grade: A

title: Up, Down, Left, Right, Hold A, Start!
text:
This is one of my favorite games to play ever. I really enjoyed the gameplay even though I don't have a controller. I simply use the directional arrows on my keyboard, and the enter key on my numeric pad serves as the "jump" button. I liked the interface of the Sega Genesis Classics program that is used to play the game. I can pause the game and save it from any point in the level. I don't recall being able to save this game at all on the original Genesis. The only thing is that the program does not recede into the background if say I open firefox and start typing a review on Amazon. :) I have to use the minimize button. But I digress.

I highly recommend this game to any Sonic fan old and new. There is no spin dash in this game, but it's still great fun. I was also happy to discover that "Up, Down, Left, Right, Hold A, Start" still works! I put this screen in a save slot so I can go back and play any level anytime I want.

I will be buying the rest of the Sonic games from Amazon.

title: Better than Hero 3. Plays great on the Wii
text:
This is a great game. A vast improvement from the latest installment, Guitar Hero 3.

The game looks and sounds great. The controls are smooth and responsive. The complaint I have is that you have to connect through the Wii remote which involves taking it out of the jacket so it will fit inside the guitar. Perhaps having a clip so it can just sit attached to the guitar would be better.

Besides the look and feel of the game, the songs sound great as they are not cheap covers. The songs are actual recordings of bands such as The Smashing Pumpkins, Wings, Beastie Boys, and Willie Nelson.

Online play is slightly clunky but if connecting through the internet you can download additional songs costing about 200 wii points ($2.00). Some songs are free.

I only played the single player mode, and have not played the full band or multiplayer version. From what I played, it is a fun, addicting game and probably the best since guitar hero 2.

title: Fantastic. Best FP RPG I've ever played
text:
This is a great game. I've played a lot of FP RPGs before and have always found the controls clunky, difficult, and it caused me to become bored with the game. This game is the exception.

This game has wonderful controls. They are fluid, intuitive, and easy to use. The Wii remote is used to aim and control object manipulations and your firing, the numchuck is used for various other items and the pairing of the two is outstanding. Utilizing the motion sensing of both the numchuck and the remote really make you feel like you're a part of the game.

The graphics are great too and are probably the best you'll see on the Wii. You can put this up against Xbox 360s and PS3s anyday.

The game play is fast and furious with great interactions on objects and easy to control maneuvers. The puzzles are fun to crack and it makes the time go by quickly.

My only complaint is the interjection of various cut scenes. They are sometimes too long. I often don't want to sit and see scenes of space marines and other action.

Overall a fun game for serious players, and those who only have a little time here and there. The best on the Wii.

title: Mionix Castor review- shark fin grey
text:
I am not a frequent gamer, but I enjoy using products endorsed by the gaming community. My Roccat Kone XTD was beginning to wear after 2 years, so I thought about replacing it with the same mouse. I decided however to try a different mouse that caters to somebody with a different grip. I don't have much to say, but I will comment on the features that are important to this group:

First_ the box. I like the way the product was presented. The box is of quality, but I would love to have it exist in just a clamshell package and a 1 page sheet with info and a link to downloads and any relevant product manual. Use the money for some other feature, like a second DPI button.

Second_ the software. It's minimalist. There are adjustments for anglesnap and many other features. I like that you can control the number of steps. The Roccat however, the software just blows me away. It tracks every click and turns it into awards when certain milestones are reached. It's fun. You can use this information in your gameplay, and it's kind of fun. Oh, I've said that already, lol.

Third_ the building materials. The surface is kind of a rubberized material. IDK if it contains latex. It is comfortable, but I still prefer the build of the Roccat. This surface retains heat from the user's hand and with use is warm to the touch. The buttons are LOUD. The clicks feel of quality. I prefer the clicks of the Omron switches. I like the braided cord. The mouse however is too light. I am however used to the Roccat which is larger and has added weights.

Fourth_ ergonomics. I have a small hand. The mouse feels a little small, but I'm a palm grip user. I bought this because I thought it was good looking and I wanted something different that would make me want to use other grips. The forward button is a little hard to reach. The scroll feels of quality and the clicks are distinct, but it's a little small. I noticed now that you can't click the mouse wheel right and left. There are grooves that support your last two fingers, however.The Roccat lacks these grooves, but the height prevents your fingers from touching. The Castor is a little slippery, which makes the lift and drop technique possible.

It is quite comfortable, but the biggest flaw (to me) is the lack of height from the heel, but this comes from a person who prefers a palm grip. This is a fingertip style mouse, which the Roccat does quite well. Claw grip work best with tiny notebook style mice. FOUR stars **** . I would not buy again, but I think it's a good buy, especially at the now lower 38 dollar price tag. Enjoy! I hope I was helpful.

title: Roccat Kone XTD
text:
Let me start off by saying, this is a BIG mouse. It is long and wide.

In the realm of "gaming" mouses (I don't game) there are many options, but there are few with a tilting scroll wheel. That severely limited my choices and is what made me pull the trigger on this. I love the texture, the lights, and the responsiveness of this mouse. The mouse is ever so slightly big for my hand, but it is a right handed grip which kind of tells your hand exactly where to go. The scroll wheel feels of quality, but it is quite stiff. The cord is braided and light and you can barely tell it is there.

My previous mice were a Logitech M510 and LX8 cordless mouse. These were smaller and ambidextrous and I found the grip to be perfect. In fact I just came across a mouse called the M500 which is corded and has all the features I like. I may in-fact purchase that one too.

Edit:I have used the mouse for a few additional weeks and it has grown on me. My older mouse makes my hand feel like cramping when I use it. I however keep my old M510 nearby in case I feel like using the claw grip, but compared to this one it seems so inaccurate and unresponsive. I am changing my review from 4 stars to 5 stars.____ This is a "palm grip" mouse, no question about that. But I can move my hand back and still use a claw grip if I so choose, and it feels comfortable.

Choosing a mouse without trying it first is difficult. You can read reviews and they can give you some insight, but it is a subjective experience. This is definitely one of the ones you should try, along with a few other names like the death adder.

Edit: I've had this for 3 1/2 years and it's still the best I've used. The forward and back buttons are in the perfect spot. The DPI buttons are conveniently located. I initially liked the Deathadder, but I now think it's crap. It feels cheap, the button clicks feel cheap, and the forward and back buttons both double and triple click. I haven't owned enough mouses to comment on the sensor as some say there are better ones, but it feels 100% accurate for me. I would say that a corded mouse is infinitely better than a wireless one.

With smaller mouses I tend to rest the heel of my hand on the desk and it causes me wrist and finger pain. This allows me to keep my wrist straight.

text:
I got the product on time, and it plays great. I actually love the 2DS, because it's far more comfortable than the 3DS or 3DS XL to hold, especially if you have large hands. If you buy trigger grips for it (available at gamestop, at least?), it becomes even more comfortable. I bought the 2DS mostly to play Super Smash Bros, but I have been exploring other 3DS games more than I expected. The 2DS is way better for Smash than the 3DS in my opinion, and the trigger grips make it almost as comfortable as a gamecube controller.

I still find it fairly pocketable in hoodie weather and winter, since I can shove it easily into any pocket. It may be a bit more troublesome to carry during the summer, but even then it fits in most of my pants, albeit barely. I don't miss the 3D at all, and in fact, the screen seems brighter than any 3DS I've used, at highest brightness.

All in all, I would highly recommend this product.

title: Myst - the most unforgettable computer game ever!
text:
Of all the computer games I have ever played, the one that I remember most fondly, and that I wish I could own again the most, is Myst.

Myst is fascinating in many ways. The story behind it is unique, but unravels with great mysteriouness. The worlds that you are taken to in the game are beyond belief in the realism to them. There are a lot of mysteries about Myst, which are solvable by completing various intriguing puzzles throughout the game.

My memory of Myst consists of memories of beautiful landscapes, amazing worlds, secret passageways, questions, and exciting answers. Myst is a game that will suck you in and make you feel like you are actually there. It is different from any game you have ever played - it isn't point and shoot, answers aren't given to you easily, and never have I seen graphics so stunning - I have wished many times that the places in Myst really did exist.

If you like solving puzzles, are willing to play something challenging, and/or are looking for game unlike any other, Myst is the game for you. The experience of playing Myst is utterly unforgettable - Myst is enchanting!

title: Mostly great!
text:
Some people have complained about the weight of this headset, but so far it's been pretty comfortable for 2-hour gaming sessions.

This is a wireless VR headset, so everything is onboard---and that's why it's a little heavy. The games are stored in memory in the headset itself, and capacity isn't upgradeable. Keep that in mind when you are making a decision between the 64 and 128GB model.

Setup is easy. You will need a phone to download and use the app for setup and to get games. Then follow the instructions and in minutes you're ready to play.

Graphics aren't going to rival PC or console games---they're a little bit retro in terms of resolution, but that kind of comes with the territory and the small built-in screens in the headset. Besides, that might be a good thing when it comes to VR. If the the graphics are too good, things might get a little "uncanny valley" and not so fun to play for long. That's not a complaint, just a personal opinion.

The wirelessness is a huge convenience during gameplay---you won't feel a cord brushing against your arms or running down your back. And the controllers are responsive with no noticeable lag. Battery life is good enough for a several-hours-long gaming session.

Game availability is coming around, but isn't really vast yet. Maybe the prices of games will come down as more are brought to market.

title: Great audio in and out, could use a mixamp or preamp for game consoles
text:
Didn't get off to a good start with this headset--one earpiece had a short. A $200+ headset with a short right out of the box? That's not so good. A little twist of the wire fixed it, but still...

The good news is it sounds great with an iPhone, iPad, Mac, or PC. Compliments were received for the mic quality (Sennheiser says it is broadcast quality) even when using it for phone calls.

The not-so-good news is the audio is lacking when connected to a Playstation or Xbox through the game controller.

It's more a problem with the audio outputs of the game consoles than the headset. It's going to take a little more than just plug and play to get the max out of this headset. Without that, you might as well use a $40 headset that is actually plug and play in console controllers.

It really needs a mixamp or preamp (preferably one with adjustable EQ) in the game console audio chain to bring it to its full potential. If you don't have one or don't plan to get one, another reviewer suggested going with the Game One by Sennheiser.

Otherwise, it is a comfortable headset, one that can be worn for hours.

Apart from the short, the build quality is high and audio quality, both in the speakers and mic, is outstanding.

title: It's a winner
text:
I had been interested in mechanical keyboards for a long time, but honestly I didn’t really know what to expect. From the moment I pulled this thing out of the box I could instantly tell it was a very high quality piece of hardware. It has a metal frame with very solid keys. I eagerly plugged it in and connected my mouse through the port extension on the back of the keyboard.

There was a solid, deep red glow emanating from the keys. Very impressive. Typing on it is pure joy, despite quite a long learning curve. I don’t mind the adjustment because it's so pleasing to type on something so well made. The reason why it’s taken a while to adjust is because the Rapidfire indicates extreme sensitivity of the keys – if they travel just over a millimeter they will signal a keystroke. This means you have to be accurate and not attack your keyboard like you would with a cheaper brand. The backspace key posed the largest problem when browsing, as just north of it F11 triggers full screen browsing and F12 opens the source examine pane in Chrome. A little adjustment is all it took and now I’m learning to quickly and accurately graze the keys in order to type instead of bottoming out. It truly is a joy to type on the K70 Rapidfire.

It’s very comfortable to type on this keyboard. I usually don’t keep the included wrist rest attached unless I have some heavy word processing to do. It doesn’t seem like it adds much ergonomically, but it makes a huge difference when cranking out detailed reviews for Amazon :D (I’m on it right now).

Regarding the RGB indicated in the name, it’s a nod to the LED Array under the keys, and I’ve only mentioned the ominous red embers. In order to truly make use of these functions you need to get on Corsair’s website and download the Corsair Utility Engine (CUE) software. Be prepared when you do – the rainbow of color explosion that happens when you first fire up the CUE program is dazzling. It gives you a good idea of exactly how much control you have. It took some learning and a bit of video tutorial hunting but I learned to navigate the program and was creating my own custom color combos and animations in an afternoon – This is especially helpful to label hotkeys for your commonly used programs.

Protip: You can download presets for the K70 Rapidfire, but many won’t work by default. Once you download the *.prf files you’ll need to use a program like Notepad++ to open and edit the name of the hardware in the line of code that says modelName>K70 RGB RAPIDFIRE</modelName – Make sure it has this modelname (I know the K70 standard models work, but others may too) This is a new keyboard and it doesn’t have many presets yet, but the ones I use from other models that look great are Poison, Knight Rider, Hologram, and Sonar.

The only problem that I have with this keyboard is that it’s spoiled me rotten. Look how much I typed in this review xD. I’m going to have to replace my keyboards at the office too :P

5 stars. Get one. You won’t regret it.

(Btw, one sexy feature I forgot to mention that I’m crazy about is the knurled metal wheel in the top right hand corner that controls the volume. It looks really cool and feels great to use. It’s the only control that’s not assignable on this keyboard and it doesn’t need to be. It’s absolutely perfect the way it is.)

title: Ooooh Shiney!!!
text:
I'm using this controller to play Steam games – it’s wired and came with a 10 ft USB cable so that made it an easy decision. I don’t have a use for most of the functions, even though it’s incredibly capable and I gave all of them a test drive.

The learning curve for using the features is a little steep at first, but I got used to programming it pretty quickly. First off the customizable prismatic pipe color is really awesome. It will lock to basically any neon color in the spectrum, so I was able to make it match my shoes, desktop, or whatever gaming interface I was using at the time. You can also map the multiwheels under the controller to different functions, which I found convenient in more complex RPGs. You can also customize the rumble feature and the led lights on the inside of the controller.

The software works independently of the XBOX ONE, so I was able to manipulate the functions of it as long as it was plugged in.

The aesthetics of this thing are really great – as far as the function goes it’s stellar, as well. The triggers feel a little springier and cheaper than the standard XBOX ONE controllers, but I got used to them pretty quickly. Once this thing is plugged in it looks really radical, and I wasn't having any troubles with lag – all the buttons and the analog sticks are super responsive and swift.

I like this controller a lot – I’ll definitely be hanging on to it for my PC gaming.

title: Cute as heck
text:
I've had the old Nintendogs since around 2006 and loved it all the while, so when I saw this I got so incredibly excited and bought it before I had actually thought it through. Luckily, I haven't regretted the decision! it is different enough from the original to be a fun new experience, but retains some of the quality's that made me love nintendogs in the first place.
My complaints are that agility trials were replaced with dog races and those are significantly more frustrating to train your dog for. Also, you have to have those yellow cards to do obedience trials which sucks.
Other than that, it is a very cute game, the dogs have more personality and the fact that you can also have cats warms my cold heart.
If you enjoyed the original nintendogs then it's safe to assume you'all enjoy this game, and if you just really enjoy dogs and wanted some virtual puppets, this is, to me, the best pet game out there :)

title: great so far
text:
i'm new to HOG's, but i like it. i have only played the pirateville one and part of the cairo one so far, but figured i would go ahead and leave a review because i ran into a problem with it. when i tried to play the cairo game, it kept popping up that there was a trojan and AVG would delete the game without even asking me what i wanted to do. i tried uninstalling, reinstalling in different places, running as admin, restored the file out of the "virus vault"... none of that worked so i went on google and found pretty much nothing other than a couple reviews here saying others had the same problem (so i'm hoping that others will find this the same way). after playing around with AVG, i was able to click on "options" and "exclusions" under that. it wanted a pathway (which i didn't feel like getting because i was so aggravated at the time), but you can also click the "browse" button and find it that way. you can make exclusions as either files or folders, so i did both. i went under folders and put the whole mysterious adventure bundle into that one and then i did a new exclusion for files and put the cairo game in there. so far so good.

i was also able to play the game (before i figured out the exclusions) by shutting off AVG for ten minutes, but that is not recommended and as soon as the ten minutes was up, it shut down the game and deleted it again.

as for the games, so far i really like them. the pirate one moved a little slow story-wise, but that kept me busy with it for longer, so i enjoyed that. also some humorous typos that i got a good laugh out of. it wanted me to find "bait". i miss-clicked on a BAT and it accepted that lol. on another one i was looking all over the place for an elephant. i was just about to give up and use a hint, but i decided to click on the hedgehog and voila! finished the level lol. same thing with the cairo game. one was "string" when it should have been "spring"

title: Simple and boring.
text:
Very disappointing. What items to decorate a specific theme are displayed and access at the touch of a button (magnifying glass). Plus...is this all you do, is design? I'm on my third house and it's already boring! No complexity to the game at all.

UPDATE. I'm increasing it by one star, simply because I play it every day, so it can't be THAT bad. The duration of it in which I play is very short however. A couple more gripes...your character can walk only a short distance, just by the shops around the small town. You can't wander into the great outdoors to visit anyone, you can only be magically transported to a certain person's house. Also, when you pinpoint the building site of each character on a map, you are transported their immediately as well. You also don't have your own house, which seems like kinda a big oversight, that or they didn't think people would be interested in having their own houses for some reason. So, every day, you go to play and the game begins with your character already inside the shop (or is it right outside?). Very very limited freedom in this game. Also, I bought a big set of Amiibo cards. The first card was cool, I got to build an aquarium. The 2nd card however, was of a character I already have in the game and all I was allowed to do was re-decorate or decorate with whatever theme I chose. I hope I don't have a bunch of matches but it's likely I will.

title: One of the best out there...well worth the money!!!
text:
I came back to review this, and saw my original review never went through...I had rated it after a day of playing it and only gave it 2 stars!

I picked it back up a couple months ago and have played it nearly nonstop! There is SO MUCH to do in this game! You get to choose your Life, or Lives really. I started out as an Angler (fisherman) and it was really fun. Later, I almost wished I'd started off as a Paladin or Mercenary because I really needed those particular stats to beat higher "monsters". Presently, I'm at Hero rank as Angler, Paladin, Carpenter, Cook, Woodcutter, and a Master at Crafting. Honestly, I'm glad I didn't start out my "main" or first life as a crafter, carpenter, cook, or woodcutter. Maybe it's ok if you switch often into other lives like Paladin for instance. I'm finding Paladin to be probably most important as I've got the add-on content of Origin Island and the enemies are even harder to defeat.

It's charming, I love the scenery and the characters, and the fact you can buy different houses in different lands and decorate them, also there is the quick travel which helps immensely when you're striving to complete certain quests. I have played so many hours on this, and still have several lives to start still. I think sewing will be fun to make new outfits but for now I'm so busy battling I'm usually in my Paladin gear.

There is just so much to do in this game it's unbelievable. You shop, buy, sell, create, decorate, chop down trees, mine, become an alchemist, do witchcraft, craft, make furniture, battle, fish...and going to different lands makes for an amazing experience. The graphics are great and the details are amazing. As the storyline progresses as well you are able to add many different parties (like the Princess, the Dark Lord, and many others) to accompany you on your adventures. When you level up you get points you can add to you or other members in your party (like attack, intelligence, dexterity, etc). There is no shortage on what you can do!

The graphics are great and the details are amazing. As the storyline progresses as well you are able to add many different parties like the Princess, the Dark Lord, and many others to accompany you on your adventures. title: Zoinks! This is a great game!
text:
Scooby Doo First Frights is probably the most played game in our ever growing collection of Wii games. I bought this game based on the reviews, and I'm really happy I did.

Our 5 year old loves the easy game play, and can run most levels on his own, though sometimes asks for help to navigate truly tricky scenarios. My partner and I also sometimes sneak a turn on the Wii after bedtime, and this is usually the game we choose. It easily toes the line between challenging and easy...it is the goldilocks of video games. It's just right!

Collecting Scooby snacks is great fun, though I wish there were more things to purchase with them. I like the trophy system, as well, and the different costume options. I just wish there were more levels!

Definitely get this game!!

The fan works great at keeping the PS4 from overheating but I wouldn't exactly say it's quiet...not real loud either but noticeable (mostly at first then you're used to hearing it regularly). A bit like having a box fan set to low. Not a problem for us but just fyi to those expecting it to be super quiet. Also, it cycles, so it is not always running the fan.

The extra usb ports are also a nice bonus!

title: Absolutely Worth It!
text:
These games provide hours of fun (and education!) and I’m going to review each game separately so you'll know about them. Each game is easy to learn and doesn't require more than the cards to play.

The United States
Of the three, this one is my favorite. (It’s my 6-y-o nephew’s favorite too.) A great way to practice learning about the States, when they came into the Union, their size, population, number of counties, and their distance from DC. You also get a wonderful picture on each one, and a small map that shows the location of the state in the country. And there is so much more! Postal abbreviation, nickname, state flower, and more. This is probably my very favorite of all the Top Trumps games I’ve played, and I highly recommend it!

U.S. Presidents
If you are studying the presidents, this would be a great game to play. You will find yourself starting to recognize the faces of the presidents, and when they were born or took office. One of the fun facts you can choose from is the number of pets each president had. (Did you know that George Washington had 10 pets?) There is a short bio about each person, and you can see what year he died (if he’s already dead). Highly recommended.

Washington DC
While this was somewhat interesting, I found it a little more confusing and not as much fun. Yes, the pictures of the places were fun, and reading the little bit about each place was great, but I didn’t find myself interested in how much it costs, or the number of visitors and how many minutes each place took. And the Top Trumps Picks were just an opinion and not facts, so it felt a little out of place. My almost 13-y-o niece enjoys this one though. I suppose if you were planning a trip to DC it might be good to play this game and learn more about the city before you went.

Overall, this is a fun pack of three games, and I know many more hours will be spent playing these.

title: Fun Farm Game
text: I seem to be in the minority, but I think this is the best of the Farm Frenzy games.  The game involves buying animals, upgrading buildings, and producing products to sell.  You'll have to keep the farm stocked with grass and water for the animals, collect raw materials, and produce finished goods in craft buildings.  You'll also need to earn money to finance all these things, and keep predators (bears) away from your animals.  I enjoyed this game.  It's long, and you'll get plenty of gameplay for your money.  My main complaint about the game is that you have to repay to upgrade your buildings at each level.  I wish that upgrades were permanent.  There are many subsequent games in this series, but I've found those to be basically copies of this first one.

title: Some Good, Some Bad
text:
There are some really good things about this game, but there are things that I didn't like as well. This episode finds Nancy in Japan teaching English during the day and solving mysteries at night. Nancy is staying at a traditional Japanese inn, a ryokan, and it appears that there are secrets and mysteries lurking throughout. Guests have been leaving because they've been seeing ghosts, the image of a drowned woman. Nancy decides that it's up to her to determine what's going on. Her investigations reveal that every member of the family that runs the ryokan has deep, dark secrets.

The positives: I loved that Nancy went to Japan. The setting was beautiful, and it was exciting to have Nancy visit a new place. Many of the mini games focused on Japanese culture and traditions. This was a long game and I got plenty of gameplay.

The negatives: It was hard for me to find the ryokan scary. It simply wasn't all that scary, even though the action happened at night. I also found the characters fairly uninteresting. Usually these ND mysteries have some seriously bizarre characters, but these characters were, well, normal. I guess normal just isn't interesting. Because this mystery centers on a family's past, it often seems like Nancy's investigating is more intrusive than helpful. I also didn't like the way the days were set up- because of teaching Nancy is only free after 7pm.

In sum, this is a quality ND game, but by no means my favorite.

text:

title: A Few Unfortunate Changes
text: Most of the gameplay in this sequel is similar to the original- you have to clear paths to work your way through a variety of environments, while collecting the supplies and workers you need.  The reason why I gave this sequel four stars instead of five is because of the addition of several minigames that aren't very fun, and are really irritating.  MKFTP 2 includes a level in each environment in which you have to smash 100 enemies, and there's no room for error- if any reach your home you have to start again.  Between each environment you're required to fly an airship and avoid a variety of obstacles.  These levels aren't optional- you have to complete them to move through the game.  Without them I'd have given this game 5 stars.

title: A good Nancy Drew game!
text:
I quite enjoyed this installment in the Nancy Drew series. This episode finds Nancy at a winter resort in Canada, trying to track down a dangerous prankster who has been damaging the resort's property and harming guests. There are several suspects, all staying at the resort, and Nancy poses as the new maid to try and figure out who is responsible.

Generally this is a solid game- there's lots to do, and plenty of interesting scenery. The resort is not as inherently scary as some of the other places Nancy finds herself (like old mansions and dark graveyards), but there are lots of places to explore. My two main complaints were with mini-games. The first is a snowball fight you have to complete every time you want to go outside. The second is a board game called "Fox and Geese" which took forever to finish and lost its appeal long before that.

Still, I'd recommend this game, to experienced Drew players and new ones.

title: Fabulous
text:
I should start by mentioning that I really like the Carol Reed series of mystery games, and I think this is one of the better ones. These games are not really like any others on the market. They involve following Carol around her town of Norrkoping, Sweden, as she solves mysteries. This case involves the death of an artist who seems to have committed suicide, but Carol thinks that is not the case.

Gameplay involves searching through locations actually shot in Sweden- all of the art is photographs taken on location. You'll also talk to various people as you look for clues. A big part of these games is looking thoroughly through each location and taking in the atmosphere.

There were several things I particularly liked about this game. First, it has a hint system built-in, as the newer Carol Reed games do. Second, it involved searching at several old monasteries and religious ruins, which were beautiful. There's no danger of dying in this game, it's all sorting out whodunit.

My main criticism is that the two main threads of game's storyline were resolved at different times, which made it less suspenseful (and possibly less satisfying) than I would have liked. Overall, though, I was very pleased with this game. I'd rate it as the third-best of the Carol Reed series (following East Side Story and The Color of Murder).

title: Fabulous
text: This is my favorite of all of the Jojo fashion games.  The game involves travelling around the world to fashion shows and dressing models for the runway.  For each style you get a list of pointers (colors, patterns, styles) that earn you points.  You have to dress the models quickly and for maximum points, and the whole thing is great fun.  This game offers many levels.  I did find some of the levels with men's clothes uninteresting and difficult- I far preferred dressing the women.  That said, this is a great game with lots of gameplay.

title: A weak farm game
text: This game is not nearly as good as some of the other garden/farm games out there.  I found the plots/plants in this game to be very small and difficult to see, the terrain was difficult to maneuver, but most importantly, I was doing the same thing over, and over, and over again. title: Loads of Gameplay
text: This is one of the longest and most varied hidden object games I've played lately.  The storyline involves restoring the garden of an old house along with the help of Austin, the faithful butler, and the dog (you'll get to name him/her).  To raise money for garden restorations you hold yard sales, selling stuff in various rooms of a very overstuffed mansion.  People show up and indicate what they want, you have to find it as quickly as possible.  There are also hidden coins to earn more money, and a very interesting hint system, that really adds to the gameplay.  This is a game with many, many levels, and you get to make decisions about how you want the final garden to look.  Loads of fun, well worth the price.

title: My Favorite
text: I think this is quite possibly my very favorite Nancy Drew game.  Nancy is sent to Venice to track a thief who has been targeting wealthy homeowners and society events.  The thief dresses up as a phantom (hence, the phantom of Venice).  This game is long, offers fun and interesting puzzles, and has genuinely scary moments.  The scenery is also beautiful.  As far as the plot goes, it's excellent.  There are some changes from the Nancy Drew book of the same name.  All in all, this is a game well-worth playing.

title: Suitably creepy mystery
text: For fans of the Nancy Drew games, this is one of the better ones.  This game features Nancy in New Orleans trying to unlock the secrets of a creepy old mansion possibly haunted by a legendary crystal skull.  Nancy investigates the mansion, and her friend Bess handles the neighborhood around their hotel, including a voodoo supply shop.  This game has many of the elements that make Nancy Drew games great.  The setting is *really* creepy- think spooky mansion and graveyard on a rainy night.  The story is involved and gameplay is long.  This is one of the more difficult Nancy Drew games- I found some of the puzzles to be really tricky, even on the Junior Detective level.  Fans of Nancy Drew won't want to miss this one.

title: Not worth it
text: I didn't think this game was worth the money.  I love point and click adventure games, but this one was not very well executed.  The haunted castle in France setting is promising, but there's not all that much to explore in the castle.  The other characters are not all that interesting, and their dialogue seemed stilted to me.  This is also a very easy game, as these adventure games go.  Normally I find myself completely puzzled, but this game never really did that.  It's also a very linear game, mostly because there's not enough gameplay to allow for non-linear play.  In sum, if you already know you like adventure games, stick to the others- Nancy Drew, Syberia, Sherlock Holmes- all are better choices.

title: A Fun Hidden Object Adventure
text: I've played loads of hidden object games, and I enjoy them.  It's hard to be original in hidden object games these days, and I'm pleased to say that this one had enough originality that I was quite taken with it, and have played it several times.  The story line for this game involves entering dreamland to end the nightmares of a variety of individuals.  Each dreamer has a phobia that needs cleaning up.  What makes this game interesting is that each level involves traveling through several different dream worlds.  Each scene has several different portals, and once the scene is clear, you get to pick which portal you enter.  This means that at the beginning of the game you really don't know where you'll end up.  At the end, when you've more or less figured out where some of the portals go, you have some control of what scenes you play.  The scenes are nicely drawn, and there are lots of levels to complete, offering lots of gameplay for the money.  Well worth the price for hidden object fans!

title: Originality in a Crowded Genre
text: There's lots of hidden object games on the market, but this one actually does manage to do something different from the rest.  Following the plot of Fitzgerald's novel, players follow the story of Jay Gatsby and Daisy Buchanan through hidden object scenes and cut scenes.  The drawings are beautiful, and the story is faithfully rendered.  Where this game manages to be original is in the introduction of moving hidden object scenes.  Not only are there objects hidden in the cut scenes, there are also hidden object puzzles that move- players must find the objects while on the screen.  This is one of the best hidden object games I've played lately- well worth it for those who love beautifully rendered scenes and deep plots.

title: A Solid Hidden Object Game
text: This is quite a good hidden object game.  The story involves a young woman going back in time to remove objects that have wound up in the wrong places.  Gameplay involves visiting the sites important to all sorts of historical figures, including Confucius, Ben Franklin, Amelia Earhart, and the Beatles.  In each scene the player must find the pieces of important historical objects, and then replace them in their proper places (usually in a different time/place).  The scenes are well-drawn, and the objects are well-hidden without being tiny/impossible to find.  Gameplay is long on this game- there are many levels.  Players do visit the same locations multiple times, but each time the scene is shown from a different angle, thus one is never searching exactly the same scene twice.  I did find the ending of the game a bit disappointing, but it leaves the door wide open for a sequel.  Overall I thought this game was well worth the money.

title: A Good Addition to the Nancy Drew Lineup
text: This is definitely one of the better Nancy Drew games.  It's not my overall favorite, but it was definitely a good one.  This installment involves Nancy going undercover at an elite girls' school to determine who is sabotaging the top students.  Nancy lives as a student in the dorm, and investigates her suspects, who are in the running for valedictorian.  This game has its good points and its bad points.  There are lots of people to talk to, and quite a bit to do in this game, that's certainly a plus.  I did find the locations somewhat limiting- Nancy is restricted to the dorm building and library during her time at Waverly.  There are the sort of puzzles and tasks one expects in a Nancy Drew game.  Some of the characters in the game are a bit overdone, but overall, the story was engaging, and kept me interested to delineate the culprit.

title: Much Like the First, but Still Fun
text: I really enjoyed the first Lost Cases of Sherlock Holmes, so I bought the second one as soon as it was released.  I was not disappointed, and I enjoyed this game just as much as the first.  The gameplay and style are exactly the same as the first game, but the sequel offers new cases.  For those unfamiliar with the series, this is primarily a hidden object game, punctuated by logic-style puzzles at the end of each chapter.  The game features a series of Sherlock Holmes cases, and you must search a variety of locations to find clues to solve the mystery.  Each location reveals a number of potential suspects, and the conclusion involves solving a logic and memory puzzle to determine which party is guilty.  The cases are well-written, and the hidden object scenes are appropriate to the time and place in question (late-19th c. London).  The suspects are believable, and the objects one must find to discover suspects are appropriate to the story (perfume bottles for the mistress of a prominent politician, for example).  Those who enjoyed the first game will certainly want to play the second.  Don't expect innovation, just more of what made the first game fun.  This is definitely one of the more fulfilling hidden object games I've played recently.

title: One of the Easier Nancy Drew Games
text: I'm a big fan of Nancy Drew games, and The Secret of the Old Clock is a bit different from some of others.  This is the only Nancy Drew game that takes place in the past- in the 1930s.  It's also probably the easiest of the Nancy Drew games I've played.  Nancy undertakes to help her orphaned friend Emily, who has inherited her mother's inn, and fallen into a deep state of melancholy.  The inn has been experiencing strange accidents, and it's up to Nancy to figure them out.  The puzzles in this game were a bit easier than the standard Nancy Drew fare.  Also, there weren't as many locations to investigate as some other ND games.  In particular, there's very little to do in the inn, and one of the things ND games do so well is to set up spooky, old, searchable houses.  That said, the game is still fun, and this is a great ND game to start with, if one is new to the genre.

text: In many ways this is your typical time-management farm game.  You have to grow crops and harvest animal products and complete orders.  The twist with this game is that you have magical powers.  In practical terms this affects gameplay very little- instead of a toolbox to fix your broken machines, you have a bag of magic powder to sprinkle on them.  That said, the goals are challenging without being impossible, and this game offers quite a lot of gameplay for your dollar.  This is not a game to be finished in one sitting.  Overall I found it to be quite similar to Ranch Rush.  If farm games are not a passion for you, then owning one or the other may very well be sufficient.  If you love farm games and can't wait for the next one, you'll probably want both.  In any case, this is one of the better farm games on the market, and I'd recommend everyone at least give the demo a try.

title: Stepping Up the Difficulty
text: This is the fourth installment in the Mystery Case Files Series, and with it, the developers have definitely stepped up the difficulty too.  I've always found these games to be trememous value for money- they have lots of levels of play, great artwork, and the story usually keeps me engaged until the end.  Certainly the length and the fantastic artwork hold true here.  Added to the standard hidden object levels are several twists: there are secret shape-shifting objects to be found in each location, and each level ends with a fairly complicated puzzle (again, with tremendous production values).  These puzzles can be quite difficult, and I would definitely have appreciated a skip puzzle button at times, but help can be found online for those having trouble.  The one place where I found this game to not live up to earlier editions was in the storyline- it's suitably scary, but unlike, say, Prime Suspects in which you build up a list of suspects as you go, in this game you just seem to eliminate them (quite literally!) one by one.  That said, the ending is surprising, and with the more difficult hidden object scenes I still give this one a "5" even with the issues mentioned.

title: Great Mix of Humor and Hidden Objects
text: The MCF games are always high-quality, and this one is no exception.  It has excellent artwork, and objects are well-integrated into the scenes without being completely obscure.  In this game you act as an investigator trying to figure out who stole the diamond.  You investigate 20-odd suspects- and here's where we get to see some humor.  These suspects are all rather shady characters, humorously drawn, who fit into some amusing stereotypes without being offensive (think the stage diva who can't sing, the kind of shady carnival worker, the stay-at-home mom who has a side job as a bank robber).  As you investigate each character you'll find out if they have an alibi or not.  At the end of the game, you solve a final puzzle to determine which of the five is guilty.  This changes each time you play, preserving replay value.  This game is now several years old, but I remember when it came out it was leaps and bounds ahead of its time.

title: Longer gameplay and harder puzzles
text: I enjoyed the first Mortimer Beckett, and was definitely looking forward to the new one.  I was not at all disappointed.  This MB has the player travelling through time, seeking out the pieces of objects that will complete puzzles necessary to advance to the next level.  The graphics on this game are truly fantastic.  We go with Mortimer throughout time- to ancient Egypt, Camelot, a robot lab in the future, and many more.  The puzzles are harder than those in the first game, and the game was longer than the first.  Those who loved the first MB, or those who enjoy hidden object games generally should definitely try out this game.

title: Not a long game, but fun
text: The first in the Mortimer Beckett series, this hidden object game has Mortimer, a delightfully bespectacled young man, searching through his family's creepy old house, looking for pieces of the ghost machine.  Along the way he encounters a variety of amusing spirits.  Gameplay consists of finding the pieces of hidden objects (which have been broken up) until one has a complete object that then must be either put back in its place, or used to complete a task.  Artwork on this game is fantastic, and finding pieces of objects, rather than the objects themselves, adds to the challenge, and makes the game a bit more unusual.  My one complaint is the length of the game, which is rather short- I finished in less than two hours.

title: Best of the Bunch!
text: I enjoy all of the Westward games, but III is definitely the best of the bunch.  The game requires you to create a settlement in the old west.  You'll have to build homes, farms, and buildings, attract settlers, ward off bandits, and keep the settlement supplied with food, water, gold, and wood.  Westward III includes some definite improvements on earlier Westward games- you can now use the mouse controls, graphics are better, and there are new ways to extract resources from the landscape.  Westward III also has the most coherent storyline- you'll be working to reclaim land from an evil robber baron.  This is a long game,  with hours of gameplay.  Well worth the money and lots of fun.

title: Can your village survive?
text: Virtual Villagers is a great deal of fun.  The premise is that you've washed up on the island of Isola and you need to create a viable settlement.  Starting with just a few villagers, you can create a thriving village of nearly 100.  Along the way, you have to solve certain problems: how to feed yourself, educating yourself enough to make new technologies, and building new shelters.  Food is frequently the most pressing issue.  Around the beach you'll find some curious objects and spaces, which along the way, with some ingenuity, you'll discover their purpose and utility.  The player controls the villagers' lives.  It's your job to make sure the villagers are fed and happy, that they reproduce, and that they work at necessary tasks.  The game runs in real time, which means that your village keeps functioning even if you're not at the computer.  Therefore, it's extremely important to make sure your villagers are well-trained.  There are definitely some slow points in this game.  There are times when your villagers simply have to work to reach the next level, and that takes some time.  This is not a game that you can sit and play for 8 hours straight, as it runs in real time.  That said, I've found watching the village grow and trying to solve the various puzzles that are necessary to progress to be a great deal of fun.  I enjoyed this game enough that I bought the two sequels as soon as they were released.

title: Escape the Island
text: The principle of this game is that you're shipwrecked on an island, and must find a way to get off.  To do this, you have to build a society to sustain you (with food, living huts, wells), while trying to find your way off the island.  The key to getting off the island is a radio, and as you build your society you have to look around for the pieces of the radio, which are scattered across the island.  As you work your way around the island a native guide gives you tasks to complete and mini-games to play.  The concept is good enough, but the main problem with this game is that it's very repetitive: build hut, gather food, gather wood, lather, rinse, repeat.  The game needs more to it if it's going to be as long as it is, and I found that the mini-games were annoyances more than fun.  They're basically clones of popular games: there's a match 3, and a diner dash clone (but not as fun as it has minimal features).  Overall, I can't recommend this game.  It can be fun to play in small doses, but lacks the development of other games.  Virtual Villagers is MUCH better.

title: Where it all started
text: Mystery Case Files Huntsville- it's the first game in the Mystery Case Files series, and the one that created the popular Hidden Object genre.  The storyline for this game places you as a detective, trying to solve the case of the missing diamond from the Huntsville museum.  You investigate a variety of locations by looking for hidden objects.  Each location reveals a new troublemaker, and all of them seem to belong to the same crime ring.  At the end of the game you uncover the mastermind, and discover who's really behind the diamond theft.  There are many good points to this game- the storyline is a good one, and the game definitely makes you want to get to the end so that you can solve the whodunnit.  Huntsville is full of a variety of entertaining criminals who, you'll discover through the levels, seem to engage is some bizarre crimes.  Perhaps most importantly, the pictures in this game are VERY well done.  They're complex, they're funny, and the objects are well integrated into the picture- they're not just plonked on top of a background scene.  As this was the first Mystery Case files game, it's also the easiest.  If you're new to the hidden object genre or looking for a good kid's game, this is a great place to start, but it's also engaging and difficult enough that it should please everyone.  Highly recommended.

title: Disappointing
text: I am generally a big fan of hidden object games, but this one disappointed me.  The story line for this game is that you are a budding paparazzi photographer, and get sent out to capture pictures of celebrities, from a Britney Spears clone to the Loch Ness monster (yes, they use a very broad definition of celebrity).  You catch the celebrity first by finding "clues" (hidden objects) that they've been in a location.  Once you've finished that, you have to try and catch a shot of the celebrity as they dash across the screen.  I preferred the photo-taking to the hidden object stuff, mainly because the hidden objects are either ridiculously easy, or terribly difficult.  Overall, I prefer hidden object games where the objects are better assimilated into the picture, rather than a bunch of them plonked on top of a scene.  There are so many hidden object games now, I recommend looking elsewhere.

title: Great story, fun puzzles
text: This game is a combination hidden-object/brain and offers up an engaging story and gorgeous scenery to move it all along.  The game's storyline involves a woman searching for her daughter who has been captured by an evil fairy.  The characters find themselves trapped in dreams, involved with fairies- imagination runs high in this game, and those who enjoy fairy and dream-related themes will likely enjoy this.  To play the game you look through each scene for items you can pick up that allow you to further progress through the scene.  For example, if you encounter a door with a lock, you might have to find the pieces to assemble the lock.  The items to solve the puzzles can be hidden anywhere- one might be down a well, for example, so to get to it you might have to find the rope, crank, and bucket.  Crank rusty?  Then you might need to find some oil.  Your cursor indicates when you're on top of something that needs attention, and you can use the clues from these to help you know exactly what you need to find.  The game doesn't tell you what to do, and a big part of the challenge is figuring it out for yourself.  This game is not a long as most other hidden object games, but it's a great deal of fun, and I bought the sequel as soon as it came out.

title: Beautiful scenery, fun game
text: I am a fan of hidden object games generally, and I love this one.  This was the first hidden object game to give the player a 360 view, which means that you can spin around within the scene and see all parts of it, from the ground to the sky.  The storyline for the game is a Paris vacation, and in the game you get to travel around to all sorts of famous and beautiful locations, from various level of the Eiffel Tower to parks, churches, and a country mansion.  The objects are actually hidden in remastered photos of real Paris locations, so the scenery is beautiful. Do watch out when you're moving around a scene, as the picture scrolls, and if I look at it head on when moving it can produce motion sickness.  But honestly, that's not such a big deal: just look down or to the side when you scroll.  This game is lots of fun, and it's fun to replay.  This is a good game for all ages, from elementary school up to adults.

title: Razer Base Station Chroma Headset Stand
text:
This Razer Base Station Chroma Headset Stand is one of those things I don’t really need. But I’ve been thinking about getting a headphone stand for my desk for a while, just to make it look a little neater. And I love RGB lighting; everything on my desk lights up. I even have light strips attached underneath my desk and on the backs of my monitors.

The stand arrives in two pieces that sturdily click together, so it would be easier than it seems to transport this if needed, in the future. The matte black looks nice in person; I was worried the stand would pick up dust, but it’s actually a smooth plastic texture that is easy to clean.

But no matter what I try, Synapse will not recognize the stand. I’ve looked up and tried every fix I can find, with no dice. So when everything else on my desk is glowing blue or purple, this stand is doing its default rainbow thing. And look, I love rainbows, but sometimes I want everything to match!

So the stand does half of its job: it holds my headphones. But I’m really disappointed that I can’t customize its effects with Synapse. My other Razer devices connect to Synapse with no problems.

title: Corsair Glaive Pro, 18,000 DPI
text:
I’ve been using the Corsair Glaive Pro (18,000 DPI) for about a month. For comparison, I also have a Razer Basilisk and a Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum. The Logitech was my preferred mouse for a long time, but I’ve been using the Corsair almost daily instead of switching. It’s good for general use as well as gaming.

One of the biggest pluses for me is that Corsair’s software, iCUE, runs on Macs. I can customize everything, including the lighting, make macros, change the DPI, and probably other things I haven’t found yet. There’s a lot of options to explore in iCUE, but I think it’s pretty intuitive.

I like the hand feel of the mouse. I have small hands; this mouse is comfortable to use for hours at a time. Obviously, everyone has different preferences, and I’m quite picky myself. Hand feel is impossible to test when buying a mouse online. But Corsair has designed this mouse to have three different thumb grips. My Logitech mouse has adjustable weights, which requires a little fiddling. Changing the grips on the Corsair is super easy: they snap into place. title: Logitech G935 Wireless Gaming Headset
text:
I tried the Logitech G935 Wireless Gaming Headset for about two months before writing this review. I wish I liked the headset better, but after testing it, I’m still on the hunt for the perfect headset.

Currently I do most of my gaming with multiplayer Switch games, such as Splatoon 2. I have to use Discord on my computer or phone to talk with friends while we play. But I also want to hear game sounds, so the option to have dual sound inputs is what really drew me to the G935. I connected the headphones wirelessly to my computer and used the 3.5 mm cable to connect to my Switch. A bit messy, but I was willing to accept that if it worked well.

But it didn’t. No matter how many sound settings I adjusted, my voice was muffled when talking. I had better results using a normal pair of headphones and the built-in microphone on my computer!

Not to mention, finding the proper button I want to use when wearing the headset is difficult. I have to feel and count the buttons, which takes my attention out of the game and performance suffers. I suppose I’d develop some muscle memory if I used the headset for longer, but I still feel like there are too many buttons. And the volume rocker is at the bottom of the earcup, so if you take the headphones on or off, it’s really easy to change the volume and not be able to hear or get a screech in your ear.

Comfort wise, I tend to get headaches if a headset is too heavy and/or tight. About an hour was my limit for wearing the G935, or I’d have a headache from the weight of it. The earcups are actually pretty comfy and well padded, the headset is just big and I wouldn’t recommend if you have a small head.

Sound quality is good, one of the better parts of the headset. But I couldn’t find a way to adjust the volume on one source and not the other via the headset if I did dual inputs.

I just wasn’t thrilled with the G935 headset. At the level it’s designed for, I would have expected Bluetooth connectivity instead of a wireless dongle, better button design/layout, and better comfort overall, not to mention clear voice quality.

text:

title: HyperX Alloy Elite RGB Mechanical Gaming Keyboard
text:
I’m something of an odd gamer, in that I play one game (World of Warcraft) and use a MacBook Pro with an external monitor, mouse, and keyboard when I’m gaming. I know, I make absolutely no sense, but that’s how I roll.

So! I’ve tried a few mechanical keyboards since adopting my current setup. If a keyboard has fun backlighting, I’m drawn to it like a bird to a shiny object. I adore the lighting on the HyperX Alloy Elite RGB keyboard! The default is a scrolling rainbow of colors, but the onboard memory profiles include a blue mode and a red mode. Unlike Windows users, I can’t download their software to get the full customization available, but I’m satisfied with the built-in options. And I know that if someday the apocalypse happens and I switch to Windows, I will have even more options in that area.

The volume control is another one of those cool features that I really like. The scroll wheel is amazing for adjusting on the fly, such as if I can’t hear my raid leader in Discord, or my game sound is suddenly booming in my ears. I don’t have to look to adjust, which is a plus.

The keys feel amazing. The keyboard is very clicky; the first time I used it, my mom thought I was murdering the poor keyboard. But I like the noise and feel of it. If you haven’t used a mechanical keyboard before, there’s a slight adjustment period. I like the feel of the keys and the keyboard’s quick responsiveness so much that I use it for writing and other work every day, not just gaming.

HyperX included extra keys, for 1-4 and WASD. The WASD have a slight texture to them. There’s also a plastic wrist rest you can attach to the keyboard.

The only thing I’m confused about -- the keyboard has two USB connectors. Because I use a laptop, I’m limited on ports. I learned the keyboard still works with only one of the USB connectors plugged in. So I’m not sure why there are two? There is a back USB port on the keyboard, if you have the running-out-of-ports problem like me. Lastly, the USB cord is super heavy duty, very thick and braided. It’s almost 6 feet long.

title: Decent, springy, good for the price
text:
This is an all around decent keyboard, although nothing really stands out, but anything under the $100 mark for a mechanical keyboards that doesn't have major issues is a good value.

The keys are loud, clicky and super springy. All things usually like, but oh my goodness the travel on these is forever. If you have larger hands this may not be an issue, but mine are small and I felt like my fingers were sinking into my desk just to trigger the key. My typing was much slower as a result, although the keys themselves were super responsive, no miskeys or ghosting.

I will be sticking with my Razer Ornata, (runs about the same $$$) that unfortunately is not aging well but it has a nice combo of clicky with a shorter travel distance.

title: Great set, good bass clear mic
text:
This is a great headset, and the sound (even the bass) was spot on. I ran a sound check and these picked up bass at the very limits of human hearing, which is quite impressive for an $80 pair of headphones. The mic was crystal clear and did a better job of picking up my voice and blocking background noise than my Sennheisers. Playback of my voice was true, which means if you are looking for a mic that adds a richness and depth that isn't actually present in your voice, this isn't gonna do that. Your voice will sound like... you.

The only time I got any static was adjusting the volume when testing for bass, so the drivers were being stressed. Otherwise the volume wheel didn't produce any static.

If you want full noise cancellation these aren't going to get you there. I was still able to hear external noise if it was loud, like someone calling for me. But they are much better than open backed headsets, and muffled out sounds like my computer fan and traffic. They also didn't create that weird negative pressure that some noise cancelling headsets create, which was a huge relief. Personally I found these to be the perfect amount of noise cancelling, I like to know that if someone needs my attention they don't have to tap me on the shoulder to do so. Just shout above a normal speaking voice.

These are very comfortable to wear, not too heavy but not flimsy light. The ear cups are a standard size, if you have large ears and struggle with headsets in general, you may struggle with these. But I would not call them smaller than average. They were a bit warm though. So if heat is something you are looking to avoid, I would say switch to an open set instead, those are better ventilated although they don't do anything to block outside noises.

Overall this is a great headset that performs well above it's pricepoint. Which is surprising since Alienware anything is notorious for being super overpriced, lol.
